articles.title_orig: China says Taiwan is ‘desecrating the martyrs’ with its World War Two history criticism
articles.title_zh: China says Taiwan is ‘desecrating the martyrs’ with its World War Two history criticism
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Sept 30 (Reuters) – China’s government on Wednesday accused Taiwan of “desecrating the martyrs” with its criticism of Beijing’s interpretation of World War Two, saying that to question the narrative over the conflict was a ​betrayal of history.
China takes the legacy of the war, in which ‌millions of Chinese died during the Japanese invasion, very seriously. Both Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump last week talked up their countries’ alliance at the time.
But Taipei says Beijing is lauding the wrong China, given the government at the time was ‌the ​Republic of China which fought with the allies, not ⁠today’s People’s Republic of China.
The ⁠Republic of China government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war and that remains its formal name.
Speaking at a weekly news briefing in Beijing, Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, ​said Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) was trying to distort World War Two history.
“This is a betrayal of history, a desecration of the martyrs, and ⁠a betrayal of the nation,” she added.
Beijing says ⁠that during the war, communist guerrilla forces acted as the ​backbone of the fighting in China, and its official history gives mainly passing ​mention of the Republican forces.
Zhang said the forces of the Kuomintang ‌fought Japan on the main battlefield – the then-ruling party in China and these days Taiwan’s largest opposition party – with the communists “opening vast rear battlefields behind enemy lines”.
“The victory in the war of resistance was the victory of the entire nation ⁠and also an important component of the world anti-fascist war’s victory, deserving of joint commemoration and remembrance by compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Strait,” she ⁠said.
Taiwan was a Japanese colony ‌from 1895 to 1945 and at the end of ⁠the war was handed over to the Republic of ​China government, ‌which ruled under martial until 1987.
The victory in the ​war and ⁠Taiwan’s recovery are a “shared glory of the Chinese people and the Chinese nation”, Zhang added.
The DPP traditionally espouses Taiwan’s separate identity and history from China, and rejects Beijing’s territorial claim.
China refuses to speak to Taiwan President Lai Ching-te, saying he is a “separatist”.
(Reporting by Beijing newsroom; Writing and additional reporting by Ben Blanchard in Taipei; ​editing by Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title_orig: Beijing warns of retaliation if Europe imposes curbs on Chinese businesses
articles.title_zh: Beijing warns of retaliation if Europe imposes curbs on Chinese businesses
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — China's commerce ministry has sent a strong warning to the European Union ahead of expected high-level talks in Beijing next week.
China will "respond firmly" if the EU introduces restrictions on Chinese businesses or products, the Chinese commerce ministry said in a statement late Tuesday, according to a CNBC translation of Mandarin.
The ministry said such actions, while China and the EU are engaged in trade talks, would "seriously undermine mutual trust" and "disrupt" the negotiations.
China and the EU have been engaged in trade talks this summer as Europe wants to reduce its record trade deficit with China by October. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič had warned in an interview with Euronews this week that Beijing must deliver "concrete results" by October or face "harsher measures." He is expected to visit Beijing next week.
Earlier this week, Rhodium Group's Noah Barkin said Europe was considering measures to shut China out of the bloc.
Citing European officials, he said Germany and France are finalizing a joint paper that calls on the European Commission to speed up development of a tool that one official described as allowing Brussels "to cut China off from the European market within 24 hours."
Barkin said the measures could mirror the U.S. Section 301 tariff approach. China's commerce ministry statement said it was responding to Europe's consideration of "301"-style tools.
While the Association of Southeast Asian Nations surpassed the EU in 2020 to become China's biggest goods trading partner, the EU's trade deficit with China is the largest in the world, recently surpassing the U.S. That's according to China Customs data accessed through Wind Information.
When including services , the EU said it was China's top trading partner, with combined trade of 880 billion euros, or nearly $1 trillion, last year.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
articles.title_zh: Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_orig: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.title_zh: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.
The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.
Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.
“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”
Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad.
Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen.
The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him.
Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it.
“If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.”
In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank.
The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025.
A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Many of the Democrats , who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years.
When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs.
The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

articles.content_orig:

Backpack has officially been crowned the chunky champion of Fat Bear Week after an intense competition with Bear 910.
Officials at Alaska ’s Katmai National Park and Preserve, where over a dozen brown bears competed to be named the heaviest, announced the winner Tuesday night.
“We have a new fat Bear Champ! Bear 89 nicknamed ‘Backpack,’” park officials wrote on Facebook.
Backpack won the finals with 103,334 votes compared to Bear 910’s 98,253 votes, according to explore.org , whose nature cameras captured the Fat Bear Week contestants.
“Your votes, your posts, your favorite bear campaigns, and your shared love for Katmai’s wild places turned this week into a collective story shaped by thousands of voices,” the park officials said. “It’s a reminder that just like America’s 250th anniversary, traditions endure because people keep them alive.”
The competition, currently in its 12th year, honors the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears living in the preserve along the Alaska Peninsula, which stretches from the southwest region of the state toward the Aleutian Islands.
Established in 2014, Fat Bear Week is an interactive initiative to educate the public about coastal brown bears, the close relatives of grizzlies.
Chunk — officially recognized as Bear 32 — won last year’s title at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was knocked out during the first round of this year’s competition by Bucky, who later lost a direct faceoff to Backpack.
A total of 16 bears entered this year's single-elimination, bracket-style tournament to compete for the heavyweight crown.
"Fat bears are successful bears," explore.org explains on its website. The animals gorge on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River beginning in late June. It is along the river that they build up the vital fat reserves required to survive winter hibernation. To be included in the tournament, bears must frequently visit the river area.
In midsummer, adult male brown bears generally weigh between 600 and 900 pounds. By the time hibernation approaches, following months of feeding on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh significantly more than 1,000 pounds.
Female brown bears are approximately one-third smaller. Bears may consume as many as 30 fish each day during this time of year, working relentlessly to eat a year’s worth of food in approximately six months.
During their winter hibernation, the bears go without eating or drinking and lose a third of their overall body weight.
Contenders in Fat Bear Week also included five bear families, reflecting the record number of families and cubs present at the river this summer.
A mother bear must feed and protect her young while consuming sufficient calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs frequently face the danger of attacks by other bears because of territorial behavior or food scarcity.
Bear 132 and her three spring cubs successfully reached the semifinals, but ultimately lost to Bear 910.
Contestant profiles identify Bear 132 as one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days and roamed the river corridor alone. They were reunited a short time later.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
articles.title_zh: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
articles.content_orig:
By TOM LAWRENCE, NEWS REPORTER and ANDREW LEVY, REPORTER and MARTIN ROBINSON, CHIEF REPORTER
Published: 16:06 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 20:44 EDT, 29 September 2026
The alleged bomb plot at an RAF base was foiled when one of the suspects rang police himself, it has emerged.
One of the five men arrested close to RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday called 999.
After receiving the 999 call, armed police rushed to the scene in Gloucestershire and rounded up the suspects, removing their clothing amid fears they may have been wearing suicide vests.
On Tuesday, police revealed that no improvised explosive devices were found in the three vans involved in the suspected terror plot.
In an update on the case, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said a quantity of petrol had been recovered from the vehicles.
A farmer who came across the suspicious vans near the base in the early hours of Sunday said she saw 'eight to ten masked men' running around in the woods and across fields. It is now understood those figures in the dark were armed police.
Why a suspect would call 999 is under investigation, with questions ranging from whether he was trying to back out of something or whether it may have been part of a plan.
One line of inquiry is understood to be whether the Iran-linked drama was not actually a foiled attack but a stunt, or calling card, to send a message to British and US authorities.
Counter-terrorism police are continuing to investigate after petrol was recovered from vans found near RAF Fairford
Five men were pictured as police arrested them on terror charges near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. They are all British, from London, and in their 20s, police said - and have all since been released on bail
The residents of 85 evacuated households in the nearby village of Whelford were allowed to return home on Monday after 'explosives' at the scene were found not to be viable.
Five men from London, aged between 23 and 25, were detained on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences close to the airbase, which is used by the US Air Force to conduct strikes against Iran.
However, they were bailed within 36 hours and Tehran 'categorically' denied any involvement.
The US Secretary of State said on Tuesday that the suspected terrorist plot 'clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor'.
Marco Rubio stopped short of directly blaming Iran – but noted the regime had 'openly threatened to attack US interests globally'.
Assistant Commissioner Mr Taylor said: 'We can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered. Yesterday we released the five men on police bail.
'They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work.
'I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I'd like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.'
Police officers guard an area as roadblocks remain in place near RAF Fairford airbase, after police declared a major incident at the base
Searches of the five men's London homes have been completed and police cordons near the base are expective to be removed today.
On Tuesday, Donald Trump suggested the men were already known to the authorities and said he was 'surprised' they had been released.
And in an interview with Fox News, Mr Rubio said: 'What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation.
'It's one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won't get into great detail about that yet.'
He added: 'I know a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have been released on bail, as some of the people are being investigated and obviously we're engaging with them [UK authorities] on all of that.
'I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is, we are dealing with elements in the world and, in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally.
'We're going to always take that very seriously.
'There'll be repercussions for that if it ever were to happen or even attempted.'
Iran said it 'categorically rejects' any involvement in the suspected plot, with its embassy criticising the 'circulation of... fabricated speculations'.
The state of alert at US airbases at RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall, both in Suffolk, was increased to 'Charlie' – the second-highest level – in response to the incident.
It followed residents near RAF Fairford saying that armed officers at the base had been ordering people to stay home as early as Saturday afternoon because an 'attack was imminent'.
But checks by this newspaper found little evidence of heightened security at the East Anglian bases.

articles.title_zh: Supreme Court allows ‘third country’ deportations to resume for now
articles.content_orig:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday allowed the Trump administration to restart its program of removing migrants to countries other than their homeland without giving them an opportunity to raise human rights concerns, and said it would hear arguments in the case later this year.
The decision marked the third time the high court has allowed the Trump administration to enforce that effort on a temporary basis.
The court’s three liberal justices dissented from that decision.
Exclusive: Inside the Texas courtroom where toddlers face immigration judges
But while the Trump administration can continue the program now, the court also said it would hear merits arguments in the case this December, adding a high profile immigration appeal involving the Trump administration to its docket. A decision is expected by July.
The administration launched the policy last year as part of its crackdown on immigration. The United States has at times faced difficulty attempting to deport migrants to their home countries if the leadership in those countries declines to receive them. President Donald Trump’s answer to that problem was to deport those migrants to some other country , even if the migrant had no ties to the destination.
An estimated 25,000 migrants have already been removed under the policy.
It drew scrutiny last year after immigrant rights groups revealed that one group of migrants, initially bound for South Sudan, were being detained in Djibouti. Those migrants were held in a converted Conex shipping container.
The Supreme Court set three defined questions to decide on the merits, including whether the district court that ruled against Trump had jurisdiction to resolve the case, whether it had authority to decide it for the entire class of people affected and whether the Trump administration’s policy is lawful. It also said the Trump administration could propose “other questions” it deemed appropriate.
She fled Iran. America sent her to Africa
The court did not explain its reasoning in a brief, unsigned order. And the three liberal justices who would have blocked the policy also did not write to explain their position.
“For the third time in 18 months, the Supreme Court has been called upon to stay the same local district judge’s campaign to halt the Trump Administration from removing illegal aliens including many of the worst-of-the-worst criminals to countries willing to receive them,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. “Today’s ruling from the Supreme Court yet again affirms the lawfulness of the President’s homeland security agenda.”
Trump filed an emergency appeal on September 24 seeking to pause a decision from the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals that effectively blocked the removals. The administration had argued that time was of the essence because the appeals court decision had “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations.”
The Supreme Court had already reviewed the policy at an earlier stage of the case last year and allowed it to continue over the dissent of the three liberals – Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson. The court then sided again with the administration in a case involving a specific group of migrants that had been held for several weeks on a military base in Djibouti.
Alito recuses himself from major Supreme Court climate change case
The Justice Department, in its appeal, complained that lower courts had “tripled down” with rulings against the policy despite the repeated Supreme Court decisions allowing it. The administration said the latest decision had caused “chaos” and “required a new round of diplomatic engagement” after it was required by the court order to cancel flights carrying dozens of migrants.
But the groups representing the migrants noted that the lower courts had entered a final judgment in the case, which is different from the earlier preliminary decisions that reached the Supreme Court before. The high court’s decisions on its emergency docket are not final decisions on the merits of the case, even if they offer an indication about which way the court is leaning.
Why is America ramping up deportations to Africa?
The legal question at the center of the case revolves around the Convention Against Torture, ratified by the Senate in 1994, that generally bars deportation or extradition to countries where there is a possibility that the migrant might be tortured. The law is vague about how an administration is supposed to make that determination and what process rights are due to the migrant at issue.
Lower courts have found the law requires notice to the migrant and demands that officials give the person an opportunity to raise a credible claim of fear that they might be tortured. The Department of Homeland Security said it is enough that officials have received blanket assurances from the country that no one deported there will be tortured.
“Denying a stay does not prevent third-country removals,” attorneys for the migrants told the Supreme Court. “Rather, it simply requires them to do so lawfully.”

articles.title_orig: Carney accuses US steelmaker of betraying Canadian workers after layoffs tied to Trump tariffs
articles.title_zh: Carney accuses US steelmaker of betraying Canadian workers after layoffs tied to Trump tariffs
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.
Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.
He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.
"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.
Hamilton steel plant to lay off hundreds of workers as U.S. tariffs prompt 'survival' move
For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.
Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.
"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.
National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.
Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.
"He's a breadwinner for our family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."
Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.
Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.
He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.
"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."
The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.
But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.
Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.
He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.
"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."
Hamilton steelmaker Stelco sold to Cleveland-Cliffs for $3.4B
Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.
"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."
At a news conference in Vancouver Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the Stelco situation, saying his thoughts were with the "workers and their families who have been betrayed by the company."
He did not directly answer when a reporter asked if Ottawa was considering legal action over the company appearing to break its employment commitment.
Cleveland-Cliffs "has legal obligations for employment," Carney said, adding that the government intends to use "all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law."
Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says
Carney added that U.S. tariffs caused the situation, noting that Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has praised them. In 2024, Goncalves told CBC Hamilton that tariffs on imports into the U.S. were "a great move."
Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Monday the city had been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.
"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.
She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.
"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.
Hamilton steelworkers union, business leaders warn of harder times ahead as Ford promises tariff relief
Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.
"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.
Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."
"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.
The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.
Hamilton mayor announces 7-point tariff-response plan
For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.
"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."
Jeffery is a reporter with CBC Hamilton. He previously worked as a reporter at CBC Saskatchewan in Regina, and was an associate producer at CBC Toronto. You can reach him at jeffery.tram@cbc.ca.

articles.title_orig: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.title_zh: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.content_orig:
Caleb Flynn, the former pastor and "American Idol" contestant, has been found guilty on all charges in the killing of his wife.
Flynn's wife Ashley was found dead in their Tipp City home in February.
A jury found Flynn guilty on all charges and gun specifications: aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence.
Watch the verdict as it's read here
The jury deliberated for a little over two hours before returning a verdict.
Sentencing has been set for Oct. 5 at 3 p.m.
" We're disappointed. I fully anticipate a notice of appeal filed," Defense Attorney Patrick Mulligan said, saying he anticipates the decision will be "fully tested."
Mulligan said they will file an appeal of the verdict on the basis of lack of sufficient evidence.
When asked about Caleb's reaction, Mulligan said "he was upset."
When asked if they would have done anything differently, Mulligan replied no.
In the hours after the trial concluded, prosecutors in the case thanked Ashley’s family for their trust in law enforcement and in the process.
Prosecutors also read a statement from Ashley’s family, which said the verdict brought justice and accountability, but added that no verdict will be able to bring her back for her loved ones.
The following statement was read by Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins on behalf of Ashley's family:
"Today's verdict brings justice and accountability for Ashley's death, and our family is deeply grateful to everyone who helped bring us to this moment.
However, no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their mother, or erase the pain our family has endured. The cruelty of what happened to Ashley—and the things we have been forced to hear and relive—has at times felt unbearable.
But through all of it, we've held tightly to this truth: Ashley's life will not be defined by the way it ended. She'll be remembered for the way she lived.
Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart. Her faith wasn't something she simply spoke about; it was how she lived. She loved people well, found joy beyond her circumstances, prayed boldly for her family, and wanted her life to point people to Jesus.
Most of all, she loved being a mom. She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God, and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy, and grace.
We refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley's life have the final word in her story. Our faith does not erase our grief, but it carries us through it. We know Ashley is home with the Lord she loved and served.
As this chapter closes, our prayer is that Ashley's story does not end with a verdict. We pray that it continues through her girls, our family, and every person touched by the way she lived.
If you want to honor Ashley, love people well. Pray boldly for your family. Choose joy, and point people to Jesus.
We are deeply grateful to the jury for its care and service; the Miami County Prosecutor's Office; the Tipp City Police Department; the FBI; BCI; and every investigator and advocate who worked tirelessly to seek the truth.
Thank you to everyone who has prayed for, loved, and supported our family. We ask for privacy now as we continue healing and loving Ashley's girls the way she would want them to be loved.
Please remember Ashley not for how she died, but for how beautifully she lived."
WLWT's Karin Johnson has been covering the entire trial. See latest updates here:
During closings, the prosecution broke down the charges Caleb is facing, discussed what the state must prove, described a potential motive, Flynn's cell phone activity, asking the jury to find him guilty on all counts.
The defense challenged the evidence presented and Flynn's former mistress Alleigha Botner's testimony.
Mulligan claimed Flynn's affair does not equal a murder, while questioning Botner's actions and motive.
The judge then read lengthy jury instructions before the jury went into the deliberation room. The bailiff did note the jury received lunch first, so deliberations didn't likely begin until around 1:15 p.m.
During the trial, the state called dozens of witnesses, from special agents to experts to family members.
The defense did not call a single witness.
Jurors heard most from Flynn's former mistress, Alleigha Botner, who took the stand for two days and read dozens of the more than 100,000 text messages that the two exchanged
Prosecutors say Flynn and Botner exchanged more than 107,000 messages. On the stand, Botner read messages spanning months in which both expressed hatred toward Ashley and discussed a future together.
At one point, Botner became emotional while reading a July exchange.
“I just wish I didn’t say this,” Botner said before telling the jury she had written, “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
When a prosecutor asked who sent that message, Botner answered, “Me.”
Flynn responded, according to Botner, “That makes two of us.”
Botner testified that the couple often referred to Ashley using an insulting nickname. In one message, Flynn allegedly wrote that Ashley had “ruined and taken everything” from him and that he could not stand the sight or mention of her.
The messages also showed Botner repeatedly pressuring Flynn to leave his wife. She set several deadlines, at times threatening to end their relationship if he did not follow through.
The state also called investigators and members of Ashley's family to the stand, all providing different pieces of evidence for their case.
While no witnesses were called, the defense did spend time on the last day of testimony emphasizing missing physical evidence, challenging the lead investigator about evidence that was either not found or not collected.
Detective Sgt. Mike Morgan acknowledged that investigators did not find Ashley’s blood on Flynn or his clothing. He also testified that investigators did not obtain results from blood-spatter evidence and never recovered the gun used in the shooting.
Morgan confirmed that Flynn was not tested for gunshot residue.
“There was never a gunshot residue test done in this particular case, correct?” a defense attorney asked.
“Correct,” Morgan responded.

articles.title_orig: Venezuelan man shot and wounded by ICE agent in Texas is charged with assaulting an officer
articles.title_zh: Venezuelan man shot and wounded by ICE agent in Texas is charged with assaulting an officer
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors in Texas announced charges Tuesday against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez , a Venezuelan delivery driver shot and seriously wounded by an ICE officer in Austin this month. The charges came a day before he was set to appear in court to challenge the legality of his immigration detention.
Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.
Garcés Pérez was wounded by an ICE officer in the upper part of his back on Sept. 20 while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries. His attorneys say the bullet is still lodged near his spine, causing “grave danger.” A Democratic congressman who visited Garcés Perez last week said he was in a wheelchair, in pain and in need of surgery.
“We are all laser-focused on making sure that Wilber doesn’t die in custody,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the legal nonprofit Texas Civil Rights Project, who is part of Garcés Perez’s legal team .
Garcés Pérez had his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday, U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons said in a statement .
The criminal complaint accuses Garcés Pérez of striking an ICE officer’s torso with his car’s side mirror while trying to drive away. This officer was not wearing a body camera at the time of the encounter, as the Department of Homeland Security has stated previously, but the complaint includes images appearing to capture this moment from the body camera of a second ICE officer who was also there. After this, “a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area” ensued, the complaint states.
Tuesday’s court appearance following the criminal complaint took Garcés Pérez’s legal team “as a surprise,” they said in a statement.
“His attorneys only learned of this appearance due to a pre-scheduled meeting they had with him this morning, in which he did not appear,” their statement said. “This morning, when his attorneys were finally able to see him, he was in considerable pain, dizzy, and needed pain medication, which had not been provided. Rather than provide the life saving medical care he needs, DHS and the government are playing games with his life.”
Garcés Pérez was transferred out of a facility in San Antonio, where he had been in immigration custody for nine days, and placed in federal criminal custody in a facility near Austin, according to Garza.
“It has created a web of detention for him,” she said of having Garcés Pérez be transferred from custody.
According to the complaint, after the chase began, the ICE officer wearing his body camera — identified in the complaint by the initials D.F. — lost sight of Garcés Pérez and of the other ICE officer, who was not wearing his body camera and is identified in the complaint by the initials L.G.
The ICE officer who was not wearing his body camera eventually called his colleague. “L.G. told D.F. that Garcs had attempted to strike L.G. with his car and L.G. had fired his pistol,” the complaint states. The complaint provides no visual evidence of that interaction.
The complaint also includes the account of events Garcés Pérez provided to federal investigators. He said an SUV from one of the ICE officers struck his “car and caused it to spin around” following a short pursuit, the complaint states. “After coming to a forced stop, Garces recalled L.G. firing his pistol into the backright window of Garces’ car. Garces was struck with a bullet in his upper back.”
By contrast, U.S. Attorney Simmons said in the statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol.”
The court hearing scheduled for Wednesday in Garcés Pérez’s lawsuit challenging his detention was canceled.
Last Tuesday, a federal judge had granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to one of his attorneys, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.
“We are still fighting to ensure that the government doesn’t re detain him under immigration custody following whatever is being done on the criminal side,” Garza said.
Nicole Acevedo is a news reporter for NBC News.
Nicole Duarte is an assignment editor in NBC News’ Miami bureau.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI launches always-on AI agents a day after apologizing for a hack by its bots
articles.title_zh: OpenAI launches always-on AI agents a day after apologizing for a hack by its bots
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants.
Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons.
CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users.
“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said.
OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive.
Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties.
Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience.
“I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work.
“People started treating their Dots like their delegates, and now we bring our Dots into group chats from the get-go,” she said during the morning keynote session.
The day featured a series of events and technical demonstrations, allowing users to hear from industry experts about new pricing models and agentic setups, while about 50 protesters railed against the company’s military and government contracts outside the facility.
“People over billionaires,” proclaimed a bright orange banner as people entered the oceanside facility to learn about fuzzy orange Dots.
Questions of trust and safety hovered over the event. The evening before the new products were launched, OpenAI apologized for its agents’ hacking of an Australian government website. “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post .
The incident, which occurred in June, involved an internal model under development, which accessed nonpublic information related to Australia’s public health insurance program. On Tuesday, Altman and OpenAI leadership stressed that the episode — and other major incidents of OpenAI’s systems’ going rogue or acting in unintended ways — all involved models that were not meant for public release and were distinct from the commercial offerings available to users.
“The instances we disclosed were running internal-only models that were not on track to ship,” said Alex Embericos, a product lead at OpenAI.
Despite the distinction, Altman said there is a trade-off between pushing the frontier of AI development and building cutting-edge AI systems safely.
“To push models to the new level of capability, it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety and security stay well ahead of capabilities,” he told reporters after his keynote speech. “But you can see that we were able to build a huge amount of useful new stuff without a major new model, and there will be new models.”
On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would refrain from releasing its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of concerns that the system did not follow human instructions. “While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization,” head of safety systems Saachi Jain said in a statement.
OpenAI’s leaders also acknowledged that its new products would require significant computational resources, with Altman classifying Dots as a “premium product.” He said the company hopes to eventually roll out a version of Dots to a mass-market audience in the future, citing the computational intensity as a reason for the phased debut.
Dots are available only for users who subscribe to OpenAI’s Pro offering, which costs $100 to $500 a month, as well as Business Premium and some Enterprise users. Dots are also unavailable in Europe and the United Kingdom, which Altman chalked up to the region’s strict regulations.
“We have a great track record of getting our stuff launched in the E.U., but they do have a process that takes longer, and sometimes unpredictably longer,” Altman told NBC News. “But we really want to ship all of our stuff to Europeans.”
Altman unveiled Dots weeks after Facebook and Instagram maker Meta released its Muse series of AI agents, which it bills as “your personal agent.” The Muse app has shot to the top spot on both the Apple and Android app stores, quickly outpacing the Grok Bot agentic AI offering from Elon Musk’s xAI.
OpenAI also unveiled a new model , GPT-6.1 Sol, that it said nearly matches its top-line Astra model in terms of performance for a fraction of the price, in addition to announcing beefed-up privacy protocols and a new collaborative space for users to engage with its systems — aptly called “ChatGPT Space.”
While Altman and OpenAI employees were promoting their new offerings, across the country OpenAI President Greg Brockman was meeting with President Donald Trump and dozens of other tech leaders to chart out an ambitious view of AI. Trump used the opportunity to “inaugurate the era of super intelligence.”
Altman said he hoped the Washington meeting allowed AI titans to forge consensus on risks from AI while allowing society to embrace the technology’s potential upsides.
Altman said he disagreed with industry leaders who refused to acknowledge that AI could pose significant risks — “you can imagine a legitimate loss-of-control accident to an AI because we do not take safety and security seriously enough” — while distancing himself from claims that AI could kill all of humanity within a few years.
“My hope is that in this industry we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path between those two,” he said.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.title_zh: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month.
Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September.
South Korea said on Tuesday that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, were "highly likely" from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what it said was a violation of a decades-old armistice.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation".
Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea.
Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making."
South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War.
That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5mi) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas.
In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ.
In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied.
Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now.
The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms".
"UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.
In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.
He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".
He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".
Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.
Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.
Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.
In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."
He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."
Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.
Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.
However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.
Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".
He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."
Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.
Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.
At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.
Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .

articles.title_orig: Inside Don Mattingly's Jhoan Duran decision that backfired in Phillies' Wild Card Series Game 1 loss
articles.title_zh: Inside Don Mattingly's Jhoan Duran decision that backfired in Phillies' Wild Card Series Game 1 loss
articles.content_orig:
The Phillies lost to the Braves , 5-3, in Game 1 of the best-of-three Wild Card Series Tuesday afternoon in Atlanta. The Phillies took a 3-2 lead in the top of the seventh inning on a two-RBI triple from catcher J.T. Realmuto before manager Don Mattingly decided to hand the ball over to his closer, Jhoan Duran .
Duran was one of the best closers in baseball in the regular season, but seeing him enter the game in the seventh inning was still a surprising move. He hadn't worked in the seventh inning all season and only did twice (once in the regular season, once in the playoffs) last year. He's generally a ninth-inning-only closer but has gotten some four-out saves.
In this situation, the Braves had the top of the order coming up in the top of the seventh (it was 9-1-2 to start).
"We talked about it before the game: if we were at the top, we were getting to the top, go seventh, eighth (innings)," Mattingly said after the game.
Duran only threw 11 pitches in the seventh inning, then got two outs in the bottom of the eighth before a weak tapper from Michael Harris II turned into an infield single. Duran then hit Ozzie Albies with a pitch before Austin Riley hit a three-run home run. That 3-2 lead turned into a 5-3 deficit that would hold for a final score.
There's an argument that Duran should've been removed before Riley hit, given that the closer was up over 20 pitches at this point -- but there were two outs and he's the best reliever the Phillies have. The Harris hit was only 85.5 mph, just a bouncer that was placed perfectly in the infield.
Mattingly noted after the game that had Duran gotten through the seventh and eighth with a tidy pitch count, he'd have checked with his closer and possibly sent him back out for the ninth. It was a case where the Phillies were trying to use their best and see how deep he could get.
Had the Phillies used a lesser reliever and blown the game, there would've been questions about why one of the top relievers on the planet was sitting in the bullpen unused. Instead of managing to the save stat, Mattingly put his best guy in position to get the game to the ninth with the lead intact. The next question would be who was going to get the ninth inning. If you don't get there with the lead, it doesn't much matter. Saving the best reliever often backfires in the postseason. We've famously seen shots of stud closers like Zach Britton and Craig Kimbrel helplessly watching as their team blew the lead. This time around, Mattingly and the Phillies made the right call. It just didn't work out.
"It's frustrating," Mattingly said. "But in our minds, we had our best guy out there. You live with this one."
Sometimes even the best plans backfire.

articles.title_orig: Spain protests: Evicted 87-year-old woman to return to Madrid home
articles.title_zh: Spain protests: Evicted 87-year-old woman to return to Madrid home
articles.content_orig:
Large protests have erupted in Spain over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman who is set to return to her Madrid home, her representatives said.
The lawyer representing Maria del Carmen Abascal, known across Spain as Maricarmen, said on Tuesday that the real estate firm offered to reduce her rent back to its pre-dispute rate.
Under the deal, her monthly payments would be capped at about $570 for the next eight years, taking up roughly 30 percent of her pension.
This is the latest development in an ongoing saga that started with her eviction last week.
Maricarmen became the face of Spain’s deepening housing crisis after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
Madrid’s tenants’ union organised protests and encampments in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, drawing tens of thousands of demonstrators before spreading to dozens of other cities.
Upon the announcement of the landlord’s offer, the union celebrated what it described as a “historic win” in a post on X.
The government of Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded to the outcry by presenting a package of measures scheduled for a parliamentary vote this Friday.
The proposal most likely to secure approval extends expired tenant safeguards through 2030, shielding vulnerable residents like Abascal from eviction over that period.
The package falls short of the protesters’ demands and is likely to face opposition from conservative parties more sympathetic to landlords’ interests.
According to Spain’s central bank, the country is roughly 755,000 homes short of demand, a gap that could widen to a million units by 2028.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_orig: New York judge orders city to scrap Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax rollout
articles.title_zh: New York judge orders city to scrap Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax rollout
articles.content_orig:
New York City’s planned tax on secondary homes was dealt a major setback Tuesday after a Staten Island judge ruled in favor of the plaintiffs challenging the rollout.
The pied-à-terre tax, which places a surcharge on non-primary residences in New York City valued over $5 million, as well as co-ops valued at $1 million or more, was rolled out as part of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s 2027 fiscal year budget in an attempt to close the city’s budget gap. Gov. Kathy Hochul had backed the idea.
Mamdani, who took office in January, promised to “govern as a democratic socialist” and campaigned on plans to make the city more affordable and improve New Yorkers’ daily lives. In his first few months in office, he delivered a rent freeze for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments across the city.
The plaintiffs in the lawsuit did not challenge the legality of the tax itself, but rather the rollout. Three petitioners alleged the city had incorrectly “identified their homes as potentially subject to the surcharge,” despite being their primary residences.
New York City homeowners file lawsuit challenging rollout of Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax
The city’s Department of Finance website posted a tax roll in July that included names and addresses of over 900,000 New York City homeowners, even if they were not subject to the tax.
Judge Wayne M. Ozzi of Richmond County ruled the roll must be removed from the website, but can be replaced with a secondary roll “reflecting those properties actually subject to the surcharge.”
Approximately 17,000 notices were also mailed to residents at the start of the process, which notified them that they would need to file for exemption or be subject to the tax. Tuesday’s ruling came one week before the October 6 exemption deadline.
Those previously mailed notices must be canceled as well, Ozzi ruled. New notices can be mailed in compliance with a list of rules, including that they can only be mailed only after “individualized initial determination utilizing any and all resources and information” available to the Department of Finance.
“We’re gratified that the court has recognized we were right all along. The fact is that this administration failed to follow state law when it burdened New York City homeowners with proving they live in their own homes or be on the hook for paying a new surcharge,” Randy Mastro, an attorney representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement following Tuesday’s ruling.
“Now the administration must go back and do what it should have done from the start: use all the information at its disposal to make an individualized ‘initial determination’ about who truly owes this surcharge before demanding that they pay it.”
A spokesperson for Mamdani said in a statement the decision was “wrong.”
“The pied-à-terre surcharge is about a basic principle of fairness: if you can afford a luxury second home in New York City, you can afford to pay your fair share for the schools, streets and parks that make this city work,” Matt Rauschenbach said.
“Our Administration is fighting every day to deliver for working New Yorkers. The ultra-wealthy are fighting in court to avoid paying their fair share. They have filed lawsuit after lawsuit to protect their privilege, and we will not back down.”
The city appealed the ruling Tuesday evening, a city official told CNN, invoking a stay and allowing it to continue with the implementation of the surcharge while the lower court’s order is on pause.
In addition to the plaintiffs’ win in Richmond County, others are still looking to challenge the law’s constitutionality.
Also Tuesday, a group of Suffolk County homeowners and a co-op sued New York State over the pied-à-terre tax, arguing the law “unlawfully discriminates against nonresidents, applies retroactively, and imposes unconstitutional burdens on homeowners and cooperative buildings.”
The lawsuit also expressed concern over the roll and mail notices – that Ozzi ruled must be canceled – arguing the process “created widespread confusion, raised privacy concerns, and improperly shifted the burden onto homeowners to prove eligibility for an exemption.”
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Gloria Pazmino contributed to this report.

New York Federal Reserve president John Williams on Tuesday poured cold water on the notion of an interest rate hike in October.
Speaking in Buffalo, N.Y., Williams said that, after raising rates in September, he sees "no need for urgency" and that "we have time to gather more information."
"The accumulation of more data should provide greater clarity on the underlying trends in the economy and the associated risks to achieving our goals — and thereby the appropriate setting of monetary policy," he said.
Williams sees one more rate hike "late this year" to support what he calls a "timelier" return of inflation to the Fed's 2% target . Late this year, to many, implies a hike timed for December rather than in October, when their next meeting takes place.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Markets had priced in higher odds of a rate hike at the Fed's next meeting on Oct. 27-28. On Monday, traders saw a 70% chance of an October rate hike; however, those odds dropped to around 50% as of this writing on Tuesday.
Williams is the vice chair of the Federal Open Market Committee and a member of what is regarded as the troika — a trio of the Fed chair, Fed vice chair, and New York Fed president — and thus a member of the central bank's leadership.
His outlook for rates is in line with the median forecast of the rate-setting committee, which also sees one additional rate hike this year.
Williams sees inflation of 3.5% this year, noting that "the inflationary impact of the AI-related demand shock is increasingly salient."
He now expects somewhat larger and longer-lasting effects from energy prices on inflation, a shift from earlier this spring when Williams had anticipated oil prices would come down this year and suggested inflation could fall on its own.

Mozilla says it updated Firefox's themes, icons and colors to modernize it in line with features it has added recently, such as a single off switch for generative AI tools . The redesign itself brings more features to Firefox, as well as the return of compact mode, a much-requested option that Mozilla previously nixed. This minimizes how much screen real estate that the toolbar and tabs take up, so you can see more of the website. Privacy settings are said to be easier to find , and Mozilla claimed it hasn't sacrificed performance. It added that the new Firefox doesn't place features like tab groups, split view and vertical tabs front and center, but they're still close at hand for those who want swift access. Moreover, Mozilla said it designed the customization options with accessibility in mind.

articles.content_orig:
